checks.claim: Key: reactivity rises down the alkali metals because the single outer electron is farther out (more shells, more shielding) and comes away more easily
checks.note: Grokipedia: decreasing first ionization energies and increasing atomic radii 'facilitate easier loss of the valence electron'; inner shells screen the nucleus so effective charge stays nearly constant despite more protons. OpenStax gives the same farther-out, shielded explanation.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'more outer electrons to give away' (every alkali metal has one valence electron)
Wrong: 'nucleus has more protons, so it pulls the water apart'
checks.note: More protons are screened by the added inner shells; it is not the cause.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'atoms are heavier, so they sink'; context: Li, Na, K are less dense than water and float
checks.note: Li 0.534, Na 0.968, K 0.862 g/cm3, water 1.00. (Rb and Cs do sink, but the context names only Li, Na, K.)

checks.claim: Stem: lithium fizzes steadily, sodium faster and hotter, potassium violently, caesium explodes
checks.note: Grokipedia: lithium fizzes slowly, sodium bubbles noticeably with heat, K/Rb/Cs violent; Wikipedia Alkali metal: caesium reacts explosively.

checks.claim: Stem: fluorine is the most reactive element; halogen reactivity falls down the group, the reverse of the alkali metals
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'fluorine is the most reactive element in the periodic table'; decline down the group from 'increasing atomic size and weakening effective nuclear attraction for an additional electron'.

checks.claim: Key: its small atom pulls hardest on an electron it takes in
checks.note: Standard school explanation and true as stated (the nucleus's pull on an incoming electron is strongest in the smallest atom; fluorine is the most electronegative, 3.98). Chemist's caveat, not an error: chlorine's electron affinity is higher (3.61 eV) because of crowding in fluorine's small 2p shell, and the weak F-F bond (159 kJ/mol) also drives fluorine's reactivity (chemguide.co.uk/atoms/properties/eas.html). Keep the context away from 'releases most energy'.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'nucleus has the most protons' (F has 9, the fewest; iodine 53)
Wrong: 'gives up its outer electrons most easily' (halogens gain electrons)
Wrong: 'outer shell nearer to full than the others' (all halogens have seven valence electrons, ns2 np5)
Context: seven outer electrons, react by taking one; iodine 53 protons vs fluorine 9
Stem: neon (10 electrons) sits between fluorine (9) and sodium (11); forms no stable compound under ordinary conditions
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'No stable neutral compounds of neon exist under standard temperature and pressure conditions'; only ions (NeH+) in mass spectrometry, high-pressure clathrates (physical cages). Wikipedia Noble gas: 'a neon compound is yet to be identified'.

checks.claim: Key: outer shell full ([He] 2s2 2p6), nothing to gain or lose
Wrong: outer shell empty; nucleus uncharged (10 protons); atoms joined in pairs (neon is monatomic)
Context: F shells 2,7; Na 2,8,1; each reaches neon's arrangement; neon stays as single atoms, 'never pairs'
checks.note: Grokipedia: neon fails 'to form stable diatomic Ne2 molecules' (bond order zero); excited Ne2* forms only in electric discharges. 'Never pairs' is fine at this level.

checks.claim: Context: xenon first made to form a compound in 1962; no stable neon compound known
checks.note: Neil Bartlett, xenon hexafluoroplatinate, 1962.

checks.claim: Key: across a row more protons pull harder on the same outer shell
checks.note: Each element adds a proton; the added electron goes into the same shell and shields poorly, so the shell is drawn in.

checks.claim: Wrong: neutrons pull; electrons push shells inward; gravity
checks.note: Neutrons are uncharged; electron repulsion works outward; gravity negligible.

checks.claim: Stem: atoms grow larger down a column as shells are added
checks.note: General trend (small exceptions such as Al/Ga do not matter at this level).

checks.claim: Stem/context: sodium to chlorine shrink to about half; Na about 190 pm, Cl about 99 pm
checks.note: Grokipedia gives 190 and 99. These mix radius types (Na calculated 190 / metallic 186; Cl covalent 99, empirical 100, calculated 79), but 'about 190' and 'about 99' match the usual textbook pair (186 and 99) and every measure gives roughly half (0.42-0.56). Optional polish: 'about 186 ... about 99'.

checks.claim: Stem: in 1871 Mendeleev forecast eka-aluminium below aluminium: weight about 68, density about 6, low melting point
checks.note: Table: 68, 6.0, melting point 'Low'; Grokipedia same (68, 6.0, low).

checks.claim: Stem: Lecoq de Boisbaudran found gallium in 1875; weight 69.7, density 5.9, melts below 30 C
Key: the forecast was made before the metal was found, so it could fail
Wrong choices: proved no errors left; weight alone decides place; filled the last empty square
checks.note: Scandium 1879 and germanium 1886 came later; tellurium-iodine shows weight did not decide every place; some forecasts failed.

checks.claim: Context: first density 4.7 was off; second measurement matched the forecast
checks.note: Scholarly article on Lecoq: about 4.7 on a 64 mg piece (May 1876), then 5.90 and 5.97, mean 5.935, on fresh pure metal; Lecoq wrote that Mendeleev's forecast was 'completely verified'.

checks.claim: Context: 'Mendeleev wrote suggesting he measure again'
checks.note: Wikipedia (Gallium, History of the periodic table) and LibreTexts say Mendeleev wrote to him after the 4.7 to suggest re-measuring. But the dated sequence (redalyc; mariuscomper.uk) has Mendeleev's published Comptes rendus note of 22 November 1875 ('its density will be 5.9') BEFORE Lecoq's 4.7 of 1 May 1876, with the re-measurement (5.935) on 18 September 1876; one account (thechemistryguru.com) says the letter after the 4.7 has never been found in French or Russian archives. Safe fix, true either way: 'Mendeleev had written that its density would be 5.9, and when Lecoq de Boisbaudran measured again, on purer metal, he got 5.9.'

checks.claim: Context: scandium 1879, germanium 1886; not every forecast came true; accepted by 1890
checks.note: 'By 1890, Mendeleev's periodic table had been universally recognized as a piece of basic chemical knowledge.' Grokipedia: many of his forecasts were later disproven.

checks.claim: Stem: in 1871 eka-silicon forecast: weight about 72, density about 5.5, chloride boiling below 100 C
checks.note: Table: 72, 5.5, chloride b.p. 'Under 100 C'; Grokipedia: about 72, about 5.5, volatile chloride.

checks.claim: Stem: Winkler found germanium in 1886; weight 72.6, density 5.3, chloride boils at about 85 C
checks.note: 72.630, 5.323. GeCl4 boils at 86.5 C (Wikipedia), about 86 (Grokipedia Germanium), 84 (Grokipedia predicted elements); 'about 85' is within the spread. Optional polish: 'about 86'.

checks.claim: Key: worked out from the known elements around its gap
checks.note: Grokipedia: he used the table 'to interpolate properties from surrounding elements', from neighbours in the same group and period.

checks.claim: Wrong: spectral lines of a heated ore (that is how gallium was found, not how Mendeleev forecast); mineral weights; order of discovery
Context: between silicon and tin; argyrodite found in 1885; Winkler first thought it belonged under antimony; best confirmation up to that time
checks.note: Wikipedia: argyrodite found mid-1885 near Freiberg; Winkler 'first thought it was eka-antimony', soon convinced it was eka-silicon (Grokipedia Germanium also: tentatively 'eka-antimony'). Wikipedia predicted elements: germanium 'provided the best confirmation of the theory up to that time'.

checks.claim: Stem: 1869 table by atomic weight; tellurium before iodine though heavier; he wrote its weight must have been measured wrongly
checks.note: 1869 table lists 'Te=128?' with O, S, Se and 'J=127' with the halogens; point 7: 'Te cannot have the atomic weight 128, but rather 123-126.'

checks.claim: Key: iodine acts like chlorine and bromine
checks.note: Giunta: iodine 'placed correctly after tellurium (i.e., with the halogens)'.

checks.claim: Wrong: tellurium acts like Cl/Br; iodine acts like S/Se; a new weighing had shown tellurium lighter
checks.note: No new weighing existed in 1869; Giunta: the weights he had (Te 128, I 127) agree with today's.

checks.claim: Context: 'No new weighing backed his claim about tellurium, and none ever did'
checks.note: Wrong. Bohuslav Brauner re-weighed tellurium in 1883 and got a value near 125; Mendeleev cited it in his 1889 Faraday Lecture ('the true atomic weight of tellurium is lower than that of iodine, being near to 125'). Giunta: 'This redetermination [Brauner 1883] was erroneous, as was Mendeleev's prediction'; Brauner's later work (1889) found the higher figures. Fix: 'No sound weighing ever backed his claim (Bohuslav Brauner's of 1883 seemed to, but was wrong): tellurium (127.6) really is heavier than iodine (126.9).' Or simply: 'Later, careful weighings showed that tellurium (127.6) really is heavier than iodine (126.9).'

checks.claim: Context: tellurium 127.6, iodine 126.9; order right, weight claim wrong; puzzle waited for Moseley
Stem: Moseley fired electrons at element after element in 1913 and measured the X-rays; frequency climbed by one regular step per element
checks.note: 1913 paper (12 elements, Ca to Zn), 1914 paper (Al to Au). 'Step' is strictly in the square root of the frequency, as the context says.

checks.claim: Stem: 'his steps put it [tellurium] first, where Mendeleev had placed it'
checks.note: Moseley measured neither tellurium nor iodine: neither appears in his 1913 or 1914 tables (his L-series runs Sn, Sb, then La). He wrote: 'The order chosen for the elements is the order of the atomic weights, except in the cases of A, Co, and Te, where this clashes with the order of the chemical properties.' So he kept tellurium first for its chemistry, as Mendeleev had; his count from antimony (51) to lanthanum (57) left five places for Te, I, Xe, Cs, Ba, but did not itself order Te and I. (Wikipedia's History of the periodic table says his measurements placed Te before I; the primary paper does not bear that out.) Fix the stem, e.g.: 'Henry Moseley fired electrons at one element after another in 1913 and measured the X-rays each gave off. The X-ray frequency climbed by one regular step from each element to the next, so the table runs by a count, not by weight. Tellurium weighs more than iodine, yet in that count it comes first, where Mendeleev had placed it. What does its place tell us about tellurium?' and add to the context: 'Moseley did not measure these two himself; he kept tellurium first for its chemistry.'

checks.claim: Key: tellurium has one proton fewer than iodine (52 vs 53)
checks.note: Iodine 53 protons; tellurium 52.

checks.claim: Wrong: one neutron fewer; one shell fewer; one outer electron more
checks.note: Te's common isotopes have 74-78 neutrons vs iodine's 74; same row (5th), same shells; Te has 6 valence electrons, I has 7.

checks.claim: Context: about two in three tellurium atoms carry 76 or 78 neutrons, iodine 74
checks.note: Te-128 31.74% + Te-130 34.08% = 65.8%; iodine is only I-127 (74 neutrons).

checks.claim: Stem: early-1900s chemists could not agree how many rare earths; could not tell pure ones from mixtures; didymium proved to be two
checks.note: Wikipedia: chemists 'could not yet produce pure samples of all the rare-earth elements'; didymium a mixture of neodymium and praseodymium.

checks.claim: Stem: Moseley showed there must be exactly 15 'rare-earth metals', from lanthanum to lutetium
checks.note: NIST: the lanthanide series 'must have 15 members, no more and no less, as Moseley expressed it'; Wikipedia the same. But by today's (IUPAC) definition the rare-earth elements are 17 (the 15 lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium), so 'how many rare-earth metals ... exactly 15' can read as wrong to a chemist. Fix: 'Chemists of the early 1900s could not agree how many rare-earth metals lay between lanthanum and lutetium ... showed that there must be exactly 15, counting those two.'

checks.claim: Key: X-rays give each element one step in an unbroken count
Wrong: X-rays purify samples; weigh atoms; count neutrons
checks.note: X-ray frequency follows nuclear charge.

checks.claim: Context: number 61 still empty; X-rays found it missing from Georges Urbain's samples
checks.note: NIST: in Urbain's samples erbium, thulium, ytterbium and lutetium were present 'but the element corresponding to No. 61 was absent'.

checks.claim: Context: enlisted 1914; killed by a sniper at Gallipoli on 10 August 1915, aged 27
checks.note: Born 23 November 1887; Royal Engineers 1914; 'killed by a sniper on 10 August 1915'; aged 27.

checks.claim: Stem: Rayleigh found nitrogen from air about half a percent heavier than chemical nitrogen
checks.note: 'nitrogen produced from chemical compounds was 0.5% lighter than nitrogen from the atmosphere'; Grokipedia about 0.5%.

checks.claim: Stem: Ramsay passed air-nitrogen over heated magnesium until an unreactive residue remained
checks.note: Ramsay repeatedly passed atmospheric nitrogen over red-hot magnesium (forming magnesium nitride); residue of density about 20 not absorbed (also Encyclopedia.com Ramsay).

checks.claim: Stem: 1894, named argon from the Greek for lazy
checks.note: Announced August 1894; Greek argos, 'inactive' or 'lazy'.

checks.claim: Key: argon the first of a family the table lacked
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'this first noble gas to be discovered'; Grokipedia: 'the first noble gas identified and named'. (Helium's solar line of 1868 was not recognised as a noble gas until it was isolated in 1895.) Wikipedia Noble gas: 'an entire class of gases was missing from the periodic table'.

checks.claim: Wrong: filled a Mendeleev gap; a heavier form of nitrogen; a relative of chlorine in chlorine's column
checks.note: Its weight fitted no gap; Mendeleev's nitrogen idea was wrong; it is a noble gas, not a halogen.

checks.claim: Context: Mendeleev at first argued it was a form of nitrogen; Ramsay helium 1895; with Travers neon, krypton, xenon 1898; forecast neon (1897); new column between halogens and alkali metals; Mendeleev added it in 1902
checks.note: Wikipedia: argued 'a triatomic form of nitrogen'; Ramsay proposed 'a new group between halogens and alkali metals'; group 0 in 1902 (also Wikipedia Noble gas). Ramsay's 1897 address forecast an element of weight 20 between helium and argon (web.lemoyne.edu/GIUNTA/EA/RAMSAYann.HTML).

unit_notes: ok 6 (53c5245134, 6f30b51770, e3f97306cd, 4e67965076, 7e0b15f772, 10af583b1b), error 2 (b018ada1fa: Brauner's 1883 weighing did back Mendeleev's lower tellurium weight, wrongly; 600299b595: Moseley never measured tellurium or iodine and kept tellurium first by its chemistry), uncertain 2 (af9a1d8d25: the 'Mendeleev wrote after the 4.7' letter is unconfirmed, his published 5.9 came first; 18bcab778f: 'rare-earth metals' are 17 by today's definition, say 15 from lanthanum to lutetium counting both). Fluorine's key is the standard school explanation; chlorine has the higher electron affinity, so keep the context to 'pull', not 'energy released'.
